summary.text: A 73-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presented with 4-5 days of vomiting, nausea, constipation and a sudden, sharp bifrontal headache rated 8/10. Initial vitals showed hypotension of 68/54 mm Hg with dry mucosa and no focal neurological deficits. CT head was unremarkable, and blood tests showed hyponatremia, hypokalemia, BUN 56 mg/dL and creatinine 3.3 mg/dL.

He was admitted with an initial impression of acute kidney injury from volume depletion and received normal saline, aggressive hydration and electrolyte replacement. Blood pressure improved to 94/55 mm Hg, and over several hours the hypotension resolved with improved kidney function, although headache and nausea persisted.

Approximately 12-18 hours later he developed double vision and left-sided ptosis. MRI brain showed a 1.2 x 1.3 x 1.2 cm pituitary mass with rightward stalk displacement and mild suprasellar extension. Subsequent blood tests showed an extremely low random serum cortisol of 0.69 mcg/dl and a prolactin of 2.6 ng/ml, with TSH 0.3 mIU/ml and FT4 1.4 ng/dL, and pituitary apoplexy was diagnosed.

Intravenous hydrocortisone was infused, neurosurgery was consulted immediately, and he was transferred to a tertiary care hospital for surgical decompression. The source does not report the surgery or any later outcome.

ambiguities.issue: The Discussion calls hypotension from corticosteroid deficiency due to pituitary apoplexy, plus volume depletion from vomiting, the "likely mechanism" of acute kidney injury in this patient. This is a hedged author cause, not an asserted cause, and no cortisol-related hypotension is stated as a separate finding.

evidence.quote: The likely mechanism of acute kidney injury in this patient is hypotension due to the deficiency of corticosteroids resulting from PA and acute volume depletion due to excessive vomiting.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not record hypocortisolism or a causal link between pituitary apoplexy and acute kidney injury as an established fact.
